title: Ten Wartime Technologies at America's 250th
gist: Cogs of War announces winners of a ten-essay contest on wartime technologies that diffused into the civilian economy. The common lesson: government's innovation leverage came less from inventing than from acting as an early buyer and standard-setter committing to things markets did not yet value, and eroding that commitment (Taiwan chip concentration, Kevlar sale) carries costs.

themes.theme: Government as early buyer and standard-setter

insights.claim: Across the Cogs of War essays on wartime technologies, the government's historical role in innovation was as much buyer and standard-setter as inventor.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Defense procurement commitments can create markets that later yield large commercial payoffs.
insights.quote: Historically, the government’s role in innovation was as much a buyer and standard-setter as it was an inventor.

insights.claim: In 1936 the U.S. Army required all Air Corps engines to be designed for 100-octane fuel, letting refiners scale infrastructure before wartime demand.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Mandated standards de-risk capex for suppliers; analogous to today's defense standards for energy or chips.
insights.quote: in 1936, the Army decided that all Air Corps engines would be designed for 100-octane fuel, which gave refiners the ability to scale necessary infrastructure before wartime

insights.claim: Air Force contracts kept Texas Instruments producing integrated circuits before commercial applications drove down costs.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Government demand bridged the semiconductor industry through its early high-cost phase.
insights.quote: Air Force contracts enabled Texas Instruments to keep producing integrated circuits before commercial applications drove down costs.

insights.claim: The U.S. government owns the PALS webbing standard, allowing any vendor to make compatible gear.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Government-owned open standards widen supplier bases and reduce vendor lock-in.
insights.quote: today, the government owns the PALS webbing standard, so any vendor can make gear for it

insights.claim: In these wartime technology stories, commercial payoffs arrived later, often unexpectedly and sometimes only after decades.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Returns on defense-driven innovation are long-dated, favoring patient capital.
insights.quote: In these stories, the commercial payoff came later, often unexpectedly and sometimes after decades.

insights.claim: The essays suggest the current U.S. defense acquisition emphasis on speed and commercial solutions misses that government leverage historically came from committing early to things the market did not yet value.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Pure buy-commercial reform may underinvest in pre-market technologies that defense demand could seed.
insights.quote: the government’s leverage has historically come from committing early to things the market did not yet value

insights.claim: Erosion of government commitment helps explain why leading-edge chip fabrication concentrated in Taiwan, according to Sarah Kreps' essay.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Links Taiwan fab concentration risk to policy choices, supporting reshoring subsidies.
insights.quote: Sarah Kreps shows how leading-edge chip fabrication concentrated in Taiwan

insights.claim: Julie George's essay details how DuPont eventually sold its Kevlar business to a private-equity-owned company, cited as an example of eroding government commitment to strategic materials.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Strategic defense materials can drift to private-equity ownership, raising supply-security questions.
insights.quote: Julie George details how DuPont eventually sold its Kevlar business to a private-equity-owned company
